hint.pages: The number at the end is the start page (the end is the next start − 1); 20-35 is a range. 2.1 is a sub-chapter of 2.

hint.questions: The whole line is the question; a leading number becomes the label (P1, P2 …).
hint.items: The whole line is one unit; a leading number is the label.

facts.testingWeek: A week after studying, students who had tested themselves three times on a text remembered 61% of it; those who had read it four times remembered 40%.
facts.rereadConfidence: Students who only reread a text were the most confident they would remember it, and a week later they remembered the least. Feeling that you know is not knowing.
facts.retrievalConceptMaps: Recalling material without looking gave better results on a test a week later than drawing concept maps, even though most students expected the opposite.
facts.interleaving: When different problem types were mixed, practice went worse (60% vs 89%), but on the test a week later the score was 63% vs 20%.
facts.spacingSessions: The same problems split into two sessions a week apart gave 74% on a later test; done in one go, 49%.
facts.spacingGap: If the exam is a week away, the best time to review is about 1 to 3 days after first studying. The further away the exam, the longer the gap can be.
facts.techniquesRanking: A large review of ten study techniques rated self-testing and spaced practice the most useful, and highlighting and rereading of low use.
facts.studentsReread: In one survey, 84% of students said they study by rereading, and only 11% said they test themselves.
facts.multitasking: Brief mental blocks when switching between tasks can cost as much as 40% of productive time.
facts.interruption: In Gloria Mark's research, interrupted work that was resumed the same day waited on average 23 minutes and 15 seconds, with other tasks in between.
facts.taskSwitching: People at work switch activities about every three minutes on average. An uninterrupted session is worth more than you think.
facts.mindWandering: Our minds wander in almost half of our waking moments (46.9%), and we are less happy on average when they do.
facts.notifications: Just receiving a notification, without looking at the phone, hurt attention on a demanding task almost as much as calling or texting.
facts.mediaMultitaskers: People who constantly use several media at once are more easily distracted by irrelevant things and worse at switching between tasks.
facts.writeWorries: Ten minutes of writing about worries before an exam improved scores, most of all for students with strong test anxiety.
facts.hypercorrection: Errors made with high confidence are easier to fix: when you see the right answer, you remember it better than after a mere guess.
facts.expectTeach: When people study expecting to explain the material to someone, they recall more and in a better order, even if they never end up teaching.
facts.greenBreak: Looking at greenery for just 40 seconds, even in a picture, helped students keep their attention on a boring task.
facts.sleepAfter: Sleeping within a few hours after studying helps the material stick. A sleepless night after learning hurts recall even after catching up on sleep.
facts.wakefulRest: Ten minutes of quiet rest (no phone, no games) right after learning improved memory even a week later.
